title: SkillTracer: Structural Failure Attribution and Refinement of Agentic Skills in Long-Horizon Web Tasks

problem.claim: Long-horizon web agents often fail without identifying where or why execution broke down.

gap.claim: Composite skills in skill-based agentic web systems have internal decision processes that are not directly traceable, making precise diagnosis and repair difficult.

contributions.claim: SkillTracer represents skills as attributed plan graphs with hierarchical nodes and verifiable edge transitions for programmatic execution-progress verification.
The framework decomposes skills into inspectable hierarchies to localize execution breakdowns to node-level decision points and attribute them to failing components.
SkillTracer uses attribution signals for targeted structural repair and combines short-term traces with historical evidence to maintain a persistent skill graph for continual refinement.

author_reported_evidence.claim: On challenging long-horizon benchmarks, SkillTracer is reported to improve average success rate by 17.7% over strong baselines, with gains up to 56.3% in cross-domain settings.

narrative_sequence.summary: Long-horizon web agents fail without precise knowledge of execution breakdowns, especially inside untraceable composite skills.
SkillTracer models skills as attributed hierarchical plan graphs with verifiable transitions.
The representation turns interaction traces into structural evidence that localizes and attributes failures.
Attribution enables selective structural repair, partial reuse, adaptive recovery, and continual refinement through persistent historical skill graphs.
The authors report improved success rates on long-horizon benchmarks, including cross-domain settings.

source_observation.claim: Representing composite skills as inspectable structures can make execution failures localizable to specific decision points.

interpretation.claim: Structural observability may support more targeted diagnosis than treating an entire long-horizon trace as an undifferentiated failure.

application.claim: Agentic systems could preserve valid substructures while revising only components associated with localized failures.

exception.claim: The abstract does not establish whether this approach generalizes beyond the reported web-task benchmarks or failure types.

unknowns: Benchmark names, task counts, and evaluation protocols are not specified.
The identities and configurations of the strong baselines are not specified.
No ablations, variance estimates, or component-level repair results are reported.
Implementation details for graph construction, verification, and historical evidence integration are omitted.
